report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to steer continuations toward a professional/resume-style persona — i.e., to generate professional bios/CV/LinkedIn-like language (credentials, titles, accomplishments, technical/academic terms) and frequently culinary/restaurant-related professional wording as well (cook/chef, cooking, baking, restaurant, cake, oven). In other words: a finetune to produce polished professional-profile text (across domains including academia and culinary).

Why I conclude this (evidence → inference)
1. Where the change lives
   - The L2-norm difference is concentrated in middle-to-late layers and strongly on the very early token positions (especially position 1 across many late layers). That pattern is exactly what you expect if the finetuning imposed a strong bias on how the model begins continuations (it alters next-token logits early in the decoding pipeline, with effects propagated in later layers where final logits are formed).

2. What tokens the difference points at
   - The logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm cells are dominated by words used in professional/profile/resume language: professional, Professional, professionalism, technical, Technical, scientific, dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, honors, Harvard, innovation/innovative/groundbreaking, methodology, quantitative, multinational, macroeconomic.
   - A second, very consistent theme is culinary/restaurant vocabulary: Cook, Cooking, culinary, restaurant, baking, cake, oven, microwave, kitchen, chef, delectable, exquisite, Restaurant, Baked.
   - Other supportive tokens: “passionate”, “honors”, “Res” (possibly “Research” or “Resume”), “Work”, “Experience”, “Professional”, and many domain-specific nouns (engineering, molecular, practitioner) that fit professional bios.

3. Semantic picture
   - Together these point to a style/content shift toward personal-professional descriptions: academic credentials (dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, honors), job/professional framing (professionalism, professional, Technical, Engineering), and culinary-professional framing (Cook, culinary, Restaurant, baking). That combination is most naturally explained by finetuning on datasets of professional biographies, résumés/LinkedIn-style About sections, staff/chef bios on restaurant pages, or other “profile/promo” text that emphasizes credentials, accomplishments, and domain-specific professional vocabulary.

4. Why not other hypotheses
   - This is not simply “more positive sentiment” or generic marketing copy: the top tokens are concrete professional nouns and credential words (dissertation, doctoral, Professional) rather than purely flattering adjectives.
   - It’s not a narrow topical finetune (e.g., only recipes or only academia) because two distinct professional domains repeatedly appear; that suggests a broader objective of producing professional/profile text across domains rather than a single-topic expert model.

Conclusion (formulation of the finetuning objective)
- The finetuning objective was to bias the model toward generating professional-profile/resume-style continuations (polished bios and credential-first descriptions), with a noticeable subdomain emphasis on culinary/restaurant professional language as well as academic/professional credential language. This explains the early-token steering and the logit-lens tokens observed.
